disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c of 6.5 falls in the diabetes range, which means your blood glucose has been running higher than the healthy level for some time. Along with this, carrying body weight above the healthy range and having a family history of diabetes are important factors to pay attention to. The most valuable next steps are completing your recommended monitoring, such as fasting and post-meal blood sugar, lipid profile, and kidney function tests, staying regularly active, and following the calorie target of 1850 calories to support healthy weight management. Working closely with your doctor can help you understand these results better and build a plan that fits your life.

foods_to_eat: Leafy greens like bok choy and spinach
Brown rice and millet in small portions
Nuts and seeds like peanuts and sesame
Unsweetened soy milk and green tea
foods_to_avoid: Deep-fried items like tempura or spring rolls
Refined noodles made from white flour
plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with a lean protein like fish, tofu or chicken, and a quarter with a whole grain such as brown rice or millet in a small bowl or katori sized portion. Keep rice and noodle portions modest, around one cup cooked, to help manage blood sugar levels.
plan.hydration: Aim for about 8 glasses of water through the day. Unsweetened green tea is a good addition, but limit sugary drinks and bottled teas.
based_on: HbA1c in the diabetes range: low-glycaemic, high-fibre focus

exercise: Since you're already moderately active, aim to build toward at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, spread across most days.
Add muscle-strengthening activities on 2 days a week, such as bodyweight exercises, resistance bands, or light weights, targeting all major muscle groups.
Increase intensity or duration gradually, by about 10 percent a week, to avoid injury.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Start with 20 to 30 minutes of brisk walking 5 days a week, and build up gradually to 45 minutes a day most days of the week.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI falls in the overweight category, so gradually working toward a healthier weight through small, sustainable changes in eating habits and physical activity can help improve your HbA1c over time. Focus on steady, modest progress rather than quick fixes.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night. Keep a consistent sleep and wake time, limit screens for an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet to support better rest.
stress: Try deep breathing exercises for 5 to 10 minutes a day, such as slow inhale-exhale cycles, to help calm your nervous system.
Consider mindfulness or meditation apps, or simple grounding exercises, to manage daily stress.
Regular physical activity and good sleep also help lower stress levels over time.
behaviour_change: Track your food, activity, and sleep patterns in a journal or app to notice trends and stay motivated.
Set small, specific, and achievable goals each week, like adding one extra walk or one more vegetable serving.
Build a support network of friends, family, or online communities to help you stay consistent and accountable.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

preventive_actions: Aim for consistent daily physical activity, such as brisk walking, to help support healthy blood glucose levels
Work toward gradually reaching a healthy body weight through balanced eating and regular movement
Keep your calorie intake near the 1850 target suggested in your plan
Schedule the recommended blood tests, including fasting and post-meal glucose, lipid profile, and kidney function tests
Get a dilated eye exam and a foot check as part of routine preventive care
Monitor your blood pressure regularly since it affects overall cardiovascular health

What would be a realistic and healthy weight goal for me given my BMI?
Since I have a family history of diabetes, are there other screenings I should consider?
How does my current activity level affect my risk factors, and should I aim for more?

What signs or symptoms should prompt me to seek care sooner rather than waiting for my next appointment?
hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
